distractor_explanations.C: Those answer the identity, logging, and configuration-control questions, not where data is processed.
distractor_explanations.D: Tier and reasoning settings do not tell a reviewer where data is processed.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team scopes data residency, audit logging, and managed configuration early in a regulated project. Why does that keep the security review from stalling?

options.text: Scoping them early lets an administrator approve the review on the team's behalf before the build starts.
The three capabilities are optional extras, as a review mostly checks the quality of the model's answers.
A regulated review asks to see those capabilities, so an integration scoped for them can show what it has.
Scoping them early lets the team skip the review, as the review repeats checks the team has already passed.

questions.explanation: A financial or healthcare customer asks early about where data is processed, how access is logged, and whether an administrator can control the configuration centrally. A regulated review is in practice a request to see those three capabilities, so an integration scoped with them in mind passes by showing what it already has, while one that ignores them scrambles to add controls under deadline. Analogy: a restaurant that already keeps its fridge logs and cleaning rota can hand them to the inspector, while one that does not has to invent them that morning. The wrong options treat the capabilities as optional or approvals as transferable.

distractor_explanations.A: Scoping does not transfer approval. It prepares the evidence the reviewer will ask to inspect.
distractor_explanations.B: A regulated review is a request to see these capabilities, and their absence reads as a risk.
distractor_explanations.D: The review still happens. Early scoping means the answers already exist when the reviewer asks.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A claims workflow chains an API endpoint that receives customer submissions, a Claude Code task that reads partner web pages, and an MCP server that updates the claims system. A reviewer maps one control to each seam. Which control belongs at the entry point, where requests arrive from outside?

options.text: Input validation on the requests arriving from outside, together with the identity the call runs under in the app.
Scoping the component to least privilege and logging the system access it holds on the application's behalf.
Treating the content as data rather than as instructions, as the entry point is where fetched pages first arrive.
A PreToolUse hook that blocks the claims system's write tool, since the entry point is where writes are approved.

questions.explanation: A multi-component application has a boundary at every seam, and each seam gets the control that fits it. The entry point faces requests from outside, so its controls are input validation and the identity the call runs under. The Claude Code task's seam is the untrusted content it fetched, so the next component treats that content as data. The MCP server's seam is the system access it holds, so it is scoped to least privilege and logged.

distractor_explanations.B: That is the control for the MCP server, which holds access to the claims system.
distractor_explanations.C: Fetched pages are untrusted at the seam leaving the Claude Code task, not at the entry point.
distractor_explanations.D: The entry point does not approve writes. Its seam is the request arriving from outside the application.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team has a `deploy-prod` procedure that should run only when a developer deliberately invokes it, never because Claude decided a task matched. What should they use?

options.text: A rules file with a `paths` glob on the deploy directory, so the procedure loads just when those files are read.
A skill whose frontmatter sets `disable-model-invocation: true`, invoked directly by a developer as `/deploy-prod`.
A note in CLAUDE.md telling Claude to run the procedure just when asked, since that file loads in each session.
A skill with a deliberately vague description, so Claude rarely finds a match between the description and the task.

questions.explanation: Skills are the recommended format for both explicit and automatic invocation: you can call one directly with `/skill-name`, or Claude can load it when the request matches its description. When a workflow should run only on an explicit call, the skill's frontmatter carries `disable-model-invocation: true`. A written instruction elsewhere cannot give the same guarantee.

distractor_explanations.A: A rules file loads automatically when Claude reads a matching file, which is the opposite of explicit-only invocation.
distractor_explanations.C: An instruction in CLAUDE.md is a soft rule that can be followed inconsistently. The frontmatter setting is what makes a workflow explicit-only.
distractor_explanations.D: A vague description makes a skill unreliable to load. It does not guarantee the model will never invoke it.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team's LLM judge already returns strengths, weaknesses, and reasoning before its score. Checked against 100 human-labeled cases, it agrees with the human grade on only about half of them. What should the team do next?

options.text: Replace the judge with exact string matching, as a code grader is more accurate than a model for any kind of output.
Rely on the scores as they are, since requesting reasoning before the score already makes a judge's output defensible here.
Fix the rubric by tightening what each score means and adding a good and a bad example answer, then re-measure agreement.
Average the judge's score over several runs per case, which would make its disagreements with humans cancel out.

questions.explanation: A judge is only as trustworthy as its measured agreement with people. Calibration means running the judge on cases a human has already labeled and checking how often they agree. If agreement is low, the repair is to the rubric: define what each score means, add a good and a bad example, and measure again. Analogy: two teachers marking the same essays with different ideas of what a B means will disagree until they sit down with a marking guide and a pair of sample essays. The teacher is the judge, the marking guide is the rubric, and the sample essays are the anchor examples. Averaging more marking rounds would only repeat the same disagreement.

distractor_explanations.A: Exact match is brittle for open-ended answers, where any acceptable paraphrase fails it. It suits outputs with one correct form.
distractor_explanations.B: Reasoning anchors a score, but a judge that disagrees with humans half the time gives a number that looks rigorous and means little.
distractor_explanations.D: Averaging smooths noise but does not fix a rubric that defines scores in a way the human graders did not.
